title: AI's Double-Edged Sword: A Booming S&P 500 Hides Deep Cuts in 2026
summary: The year 2026 presented a paradoxical market, with the S&P 500 surging over 8% while ten of its own constituent stocks plummeted more than 40%. This dramatic divergence was largely driven by an insatiable investor appetite for artificial intelligence, leading to a frenzy of investment in AI-centric firms and a simultaneous, fearful divestment from companies perceived as vulnerable to AI disruption.
content:
The financial narrative of 2026 might appear straightforward at first glance: the S&P 500, that stalwart barometer of market health, climbed a respectable 8.28%. Yet, beneath this seemingly bullish surface lies a tale of profound divergence, where the rising tide lifted some boats sky-high while capsizing others entirely. Indeed, ten individual stocks within that very same index shed over 40% of their value, painting a stark picture of a market deeply fractured.

This dramatic split isn't random; it’s largely the consequence of a singular, all-consuming obsession: artificial intelligence. Investors, gripped by the transformative promise of AI, have thrown caution to the wind, pouring unprecedented sums into companies even remotely connected to the technology. Valuations once considered outlandish are now the norm, fueled by a collective belief that AI will reshape every industry, creating untold wealth for those who back the winners. This speculative fervor has created a gravitational pull, sucking capital into the AI orbit with dizzying force.

The flip side of this AI-driven exuberance is a brutal reckoning for those outside the burgeoning AI ecosystem. Companies in sectors perceived as susceptible to AI’s disruptive hammer – from traditional manufacturing and legacy software to certain service industries – have found themselves on the wrong end of a massive sell-off. Investors, seemingly operating on the principle of 'dump everything AI might kill,' have liquidated positions with alarming speed, causing once-stable enterprises to bleed value at an accelerated pace. It's a preemptive strike, driven by fear that tomorrow's AI innovations will render yesterday's business models obsolete.

While the specter of AI certainly casts a long shadow over these struggling companies, it would be an oversimplification to attribute every misfortune solely to algorithmic advancements. Underlying operational issues, shifting consumer preferences, or broader economic headwinds undoubtedly contributed to the woes of some of these market laggards. However, the sheer scale and uniformity of the downturn among non-AI stocks strongly suggest that the 'AI effect' was, for many, the primary catalyst, magnifying existing vulnerabilities into full-blown crises.

As 2026 closes the books, the S&P 500 stands as a testament to both triumph and turmoil. It’s a powerful illustration of how swiftly technological paradigms can redraw the economic landscape, creating overnight giants and leaving others scrambling for survival. The market has spoken, and its message is clear: in the age of AI, adaptability isn't just a competitive edge; it's a matter of corporate life or death.
keyTakeaways: The S&P 500 experienced a significant divergence in 2026, with overall growth masking severe declines of over 40% for ten individual stocks.
Investor enthusiasm for AI-related companies fueled massive capital inflows, creating a speculative boom across the technology sector.
Concurrently, fear of AI disruption led to a widespread sell-off in companies perceived as vulnerable, causing substantial losses for some market laggards.
author: Lockridge Okoth

title: AT&T's Ground Advantage: Why Its CEO Isn't Sweating Satellite Competition
summary: AT&T's CEO remains unfazed by the growing challenge from satellite internet providers, asserting that the company's extensive land-based infrastructure provides an insurmountable competitive edge. This deep-rooted network, built over decades, positions AT&T to withstand new market entrants despite their significant capital or technological advancements.
content:
As the cosmos increasingly becomes the next frontier for internet connectivity, with players like SpaceX's Starlink and Amazon's Project Kuiper beaming down ambitious promises, traditional telecommunications giants might seem poised for an existential threat. Yet, AT&T's CEO, John Stankey, remains remarkably unperturbed, painting a starkly different picture of the competitive landscape.

Stankey’s confidence isn't born of complacency but a profound belief in AT&T's terrestrial bedrock. He argues that very few industries in America boast an infrastructure advantage as entrenched as theirs. We're talking about a vast network of fiber optics, cellular towers, and established fixed-line connections that have taken decades, and billions of dollars, to construct, reaching nearly every corner of the nation.

This isn't merely a matter of capital investment; it's about the sheer scale of physical deployment, securing rights-of-way, navigating local regulations, maintaining a massive grid, and serving an established customer base across diverse geographies. For any newcomer, regardless of their technological prowess or deep pockets, Stankey posits it's a 'decade-long climb' simply to approach the foundational reach AT&T already commands. This perspective suggests that while satellite solutions will carve out niche markets, particularly in underserved rural areas, they face an uphill battle in directly challenging the incumbents' dominance in urban and suburban centers where infrastructure is dense and deeply integrated.

Ultimately, AT&T's executive vision suggests that while satellite internet is a fascinating technological leap, it won't easily unseat the giants whose roots run deep beneath American soil. The battle for reliable, high-speed connectivity, it seems, will continue to be fought not just in orbit, but firmly on the ground.
keyTakeaways: AT&T's CEO expresses strong confidence in the company's existing, extensive terrestrial infrastructure as a competitive advantage.
New satellite internet competitors face a 'decade-long climb' to match AT&T's deep-seated network reach and established market presence.
The inherent value lies in AT&T's vast network of fiber, cellular towers, and fixed-line connections, which represents a significant barrier to entry for disruptors.
author: Mwangi Enos
